items.english: "Who is it that is ill?" he found himself asking, before he knew it.
"It is only that I kept dreaming that our grand-master lay gravely ill, night after night, until I could bear it no longer, and so I alone slipped out and came away like this."
"What! A dream that your grand-master is ill--"

In an age of poor roads, fearing for the safety of those cut off from one presses deeper than it does now. In a world with no telegraph, no telephone, no post, the mind by itself runs to imagining. And with that, superstition cannot help but run high.

A diviner's words. A dream. A crow's cry. Even a broken sandal-thong is feared as an evil omen. And so to set out from afar to visit the sick, taking a bad dream as if it were fact, is by no means rash or heedless.
notes: Crow's cry renders karasutobi/karasu naki phrasing; the sense is a crow's call taken as omen, not certain of the exact form.

items.english: Ryujiro himself was bound for Edo on account of just such a dream, so he harboured no doubt of the girl. And at their being in the same plight, a sudden fellow feeling came over him.
"And that grand-master is--" Ryujiro asked, hastening onward all the while, of course.

"I am a travelling acrobat, one of the Takewari troupe, and I am called Kotora. The master I walk the circuits with is Takewari Toramatsu, and his master again is Takewari Toradayu, the grand-master of our art," the girl told her story for the first time.
"Ho, I had heard of the Takewari troupe."
